chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who enters Mecca with women whom he had instructed, so they performed Tamattu' before the Day of Tarwiyah by one day, or two days, or three. So he feared menstruation for some of them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'When they have completed their Tamattu' and have exited Ihram, let him look to the one whom he fears menstruation for, so he should instruct her to perform Ghusl and begin with the Hajj from her place. Then she should perform Tawaf around the House, and around As-Safa and Al-Marwa. So if something occurs with her, she completes the remainder of the rituals while being a Haidh (menstruating).'

So I said, 'Is it not so that the Tawaf of the women remains?' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'So she is held in pledge until she finishes it?' He said, 'Yes.' I said, 'So why leave her until she completes her rituals?' He said, 'One ritual remaining upon her is easier for her than if all the rituals remained upon her, out of fear of menstruation.'

I said, 'Supposing the cameleer refuses to stay with her, and the fellow travelers?' He said, 'That is not for them. She should seek their support until they stay with her, until she is pure and completes her rituals.'

key_terms.التَّمَتُّع: Tamattu' (a type of Hajj where Umrah and Hajj are performed separately)
key_terms.طَوَافُ النِّسَاء: Tawaf al-Nisa (the Tawaf performed by women)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a woman in Hajj al-Tamattu' who fears menstruation before completing all rituals?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi addresses the specific fiqh of Hajj al-Tamattu' for women who enter Ihram early and fear menstruation, establishing the principle of 'ease over hardship' by allowing them to transition to Hajj Ihram immediately after Umrah rather than waiting. The Imam clarifies that while the woman remains bound by the obligation to complete all rites, the companions are not required to wait idly, thereby preventing unnecessary delay for the group. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on practical flexibility in ritual purity laws, ensuring that the fear of missing Hajj obligations does not lead to greater religious burden.
